name: Harold Macmillan
role: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom (1957–1963)
summary: Macmillan was a Conservative prime minister who pursued economic planning within a mixed economy. He accelerated British decolonisation, applied to join the European Economic Community, and negotiated to preserve a British nuclear deterrent within the Atlantic alliance.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Macmillan agreed to build Royal Navy submarines for a British nuclear force and assign the force to Atlantic alliance defence.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: The Peerage Act initiated by Macmillan’s government retained hereditary titles and admitted hereditary peeresses in their own right to the Lords.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: As housing minister, Macmillan administered council tenancies and carried a measure permitting councils to sell or grant long leaseholds under regulated conditions.

all-land-state-owned.rationale: Macmillan carried a provision enabling council homes to be sold to individual buyers, including sitting tenants.

arms-reduction.rationale: Macmillan implemented a reduction in conventional manpower under the 1957 defence programme, retaining the forces his government considered necessary for deterrence and limited conflicts.

automate-paid-work.rationale: Macmillan proposed running automated plants continuously in shorter shifts, using the productivity gains to increase workers’ leisure.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Macmillan appointed Maudling with a brief to finance expansion and curb unemployment. The 1963 stimulus budget planned a £687 million overall deficit, up from £66 million the previous year.

build-apartments-freely.rationale: Macmillan introduced a planning reform that removed the development charge while retaining the requirement for planning permission and public authorities’ power to refuse it.

death-penalty.rationale: In the Homicide Bill committee division, Macmillan voted to retain language in the clause that classified particular murders as capital.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Macmillan formed a government at the Queen’s invitation and used the hereditary Crown’s appointment powers during the transition to his successor.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Macmillan moved to open accession negotiations with the European Economic Community, a trading bloc outside the Commonwealth.

elective-rulers.rationale: Macmillan operated the system in which the hereditary sovereign appointed the prime minister and played a formal role in the succession after his resignation.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Macmillan agreed to assign British Polaris forces to the defence of the Atlantic alliance, reserving their independent use for cases involving supreme national interests.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Macmillan backed continuation of the civil nuclear power station programme while pressure mounted to curtail it because of falling demand for coal.

force-without-un.rationale: Macmillan sent troops to Jordan at its government’s request without waiting for Security Council authorisation.

government-encourage-intercultural-conta.rationale: Macmillan told the South African Parliament that fostering fellowship between different racial groups was an aim of British policy in multiracial territories.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Macmillan negotiated for British submarines carrying British warheads and US-supplied missiles, with Britain retaining the right to use the force when it judged its supreme national interests at stake.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: Macmillan reached the Nassau Agreement to preserve Britain’s nuclear deterrent through a new Polaris force during the confrontation with the Soviet Union.

military-force-beyond-defence.rationale: Macmillan convened the Cabinet that authorised sending British troops to Jordan at its government’s request.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Macmillan accepted the Queen’s invitation to form a government and advised her on the appointment of his successor through the royal prerogative.

municipal-businesses-mixed-economy.rationale: Macmillan used subsidies to increase council housebuilding and cut development charges to encourage private building.

national-church-status.rationale: Macmillan exercised the prime minister’s part in filling the established Church of England’s senior office by choosing Michael Ramsey for Canterbury.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Macmillan used public powers and subsidies to expand housing provision as housing minister.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: Macmillan negotiated advance notice arrangements for alerts involving US forces stationed in the United Kingdom and accepted the resulting arrangements.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: Macmillan and Eisenhower reached the Bermuda agreement that led to the deployment of nuclear-armed Thor missiles in Britain.

open-borders.rationale: Macmillan’s government replaced unrestricted entry for many Commonwealth citizens with statutory border controls and a work-voucher system.

people-in-arms.rationale: Macmillan’s government phased out National Service under a defence programme that retained regular professional forces.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Macmillan moved a Commons resolution supporting a formal application under the Treaty of Rome. The motion required parliamentary approval before entering any agreement affecting British sovereignty.

price-stability-first.rationale: Macmillan replaced Selwyn Lloyd with Reginald Maudling and directed the new Chancellor to expand demand to curb unemployment after the previous deflationary programme.

property-fundamental.rationale: Macmillan introduced a planning bill that retained compulsory purchase and set the terms of compensation for land that public authorities acquired.

public-ownership.rationale: Macmillan voted for the bill that returned major iron and steel firms to private ownership while retaining public supervision of the industry.

racial-franchise.rationale: Macmillan argued in Cape Town for expanding political participation across racial communities on the basis of individual merit.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Macmillan told the Commons that apartheid turned a wrong into an official principle and described the philosophy behind it as misguided.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Macmillan’s government enacted the Commonwealth Immigrants Act, which restricted entry for Commonwealth citizens and tied many admissions to work vouchers.

results-over-ideology.rationale: In his maiden speech in the Lords, Macmillan called for pragmatic politics and criticised both laissez-faire and collectivism as rigid doctrines.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Macmillan carried a discretionary council-house sales clause that left the timing of sales to local authorities and subjected sales to ministerial consent.

second-chamber.rationale: Macmillan’s government reformed the House of Lords through life appointments and retained it as a second legislative chamber.

separate-church-state.rationale: Macmillan used his office as prime minister to select Michael Ramsey as Archbishop of Canterbury.

social-market-economy.rationale: Macmillan’s government invested in the NHS and accepted the postwar welfare state. In office he also defended and voted for the bill returning iron and steel firms to private ownership.

state-harmful.rationale: Macmillan introduced a Housing Bill that used legislation and public funding to support local authority housing provision.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Macmillan committed the British Polaris force to the Western alliance under the Nassau Agreement, with an exception for supreme national interests.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: Under Macmillan, the Hospital Plan directed public investment into the universal NHS hospital network.

universal-healthcare.rationale: The Macmillan government continued the universal NHS and committed to a programme to modernise its hospitals through the 1962 Hospital Plan.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Macmillan put legislation through the Commons to make it easier for councils to sell homes to individual buyers, including tenants.

work-centre-of-life.rationale: Macmillan welcomed the prospect that machines could take over more work and argued that people should use the resulting leisure for education, sport and other pursuits.

notes: Reviewed Commons speeches, divisions and policy announcements by membership and date, along with the Lords maiden speech, the Gutenberg catalogue, diplomatic records and domestic policy histories. Searches covered the economy and public services, parliamentary and Crown powers, military alliances, decolonisation and Commonwealth migration, civil liberties and criminal law, religion and broadcasting, pollution and energy, automation, political means and international development. The Cape Town address is cited from the portions available in the transcript.
